Essay 1 · Opinion
Prompt: Some people think schools should teach practical life skills, such as cooking and managing money,
instead of some academic subjects. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Analyze: topic: practical skills in schools · task: Give and justify a degree of agreement with replacing some
academic subjects by practical skills · parts: One question, so one position; notice the word 'instead of', which
means replacement
Position: I partly agree: practical skills deserve a place, but they should be added without replacing core
academic subjects.
Plan
Introduction Paraphrase proposal; partly agree; skills valuable but
academic foundations must stay
Body 1 C Practical lessons prepare students for independent adult
life · E Young adult with no budget spends ﬁrst salary
quickly · I Schools can produce graduates unready for daily
decisions · W Everyone eats and spends, so lessons justify
timetable space
Body 2 C Whole academic subjects should not be dropped · E
Mathematics underlies budgeting; percentages compare
loans · I Practical skills often depend on academic
knowledge · W Trim content and use projects; keeps future
options open
The other side Admittedly timetables are crowded. However, trimming and
combining subjects releases time without dropping
disciplines.
Conclusion Teach practical skills alongside academic subjects; balance
serves study and independence
Band
7-style
model
(284
words):
Some people believe that schools should teach practical skills, such as cooking and managing money, in place
of certain academic subjects. I partly agree. These skills deserve a secure place in the curriculum, but they
should be added with care rather than used to replace core academic study.
Practical lessons prepare students for the independent life that follows graduation. A young adult who has
never made a budget may spend a ﬁrst salary within a few days and then borrow money to survive the rest of
the month. This shows that a school can produce students who pass examinations but cannot manage ordinary
daily decisions. Because every person must eat, spend and save, lessons on these topics beneﬁt all students,
and this universal value justiﬁes giving them real time in the weekly timetable.
However, whole academic subjects should not be dropped to make room. Mathematics, for instance, is the
foundation of sensible budgeting, because a student who does not understand percentages cannot compare
two loan oﬀers. This suggests that many practical skills depend on academic knowledge rather than competing
with it. Admittedly, school timetables are already crowded, so adding new lessons means that something must
be reduced. Nevertheless, time can be released by trimming rarely used content inside each subject, or by

Essay 2 · Opinion
Prompt: Governments should spend more money on public transport than on building new roads. To what
extent do you agree or disagree?
Analyze: topic: public transport versus roads · task: State and support a level of agreement that governments
should spend more on public transport than on new roads · parts: One question; notice the comparison 'more
than', so both options must be weighed
Position: I agree: public transport deserves the larger share of public money because it serves more people
and solves problems that new roads create.
Plan
Introduction Governments choose between new roads and public
transport; agree transport deserves more because it serves
more people
Body 1 C Public transport moves many people eﬃciently · E One
train carries as many commuters as dozens of cars · I
Investment eases congestion for drivers too · W City land is
limited, so eﬃcient space use comes ﬁrst
Body 2 C New roads soon ﬁll with traﬃc · E Wider motorway
attracts more drivers; queues return · I Road building treats
symptom, not cause · W Maintain roads cheaply; spend rest
where most citizens beneﬁt
The other side Admittedly rural areas cannot support regular buses or
trains. However, that justiﬁes maintenance, not new
construction.
Conclusion Transport spending should be prioritised; roads only
maintained
Band
7-style
model
(267
words):
Governments often have to choose between building new roads and improving buses, trains and trams. I agree
that public transport should receive the larger share of public money, because it serves more people and avoids
problems that new roads tend to create.
Public transport moves large numbers of passengers eﬃciently. A single train can carry as many commuters as
dozens of cars, and it occupies far less space in a crowded city centre. This means that investment in rail lines
or dedicated bus lanes can ease congestion for everyone, including those who continue to drive. Since land in
cities is limited, the form of transport that uses space most eﬃciently is the one that should be funded ﬁrst.
New roads, by contrast, tend to ﬁll with traﬃc soon after they open. A wider motorway, for example, often
attracts drivers who previously stayed at home or chose another route, so the queues return within a short time.
This indicates that road building treats the symptom of congestion rather than its cause. Admittedly, some
regions, particularly rural areas, have too few residents to support frequent buses or trains, and people there
depend on cars. However, this is a reason to keep existing roads in good repair, not to build many new ones,
and a modest maintenance budget costs far less than a major construction programme. The remaining money
is better spent where it will serve the greatest number of citizens every day.
